# Parallax Science Shorts — Complete Knowledge Base

> Full transcripts, Q&A explanations, and peer-reviewed sources for all published Parallax Science Shorts.

## Do People Notice Your Embarrassment? (The T-Shirt Test)
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/spotlight_effect/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/MrHJXgyATk8
- Transcript: You risk hiding after 1 blush and 1 glance. But before you blame them, what did researchers check? Replay that awkward moment. Your face burns; surely the room registered it. Predict: half the room, or fewer? In a 2000 experiment, students wore a potentially embarrassing Barry Manilow T-shirt into a room. They expected roughly half the observers to identify him. Would you bet lower? But here's the strange part: feeling exposed wasn't evidence that anyone remembered. The uncomfortable possibility: your embarrassment can inflate your estimate of other people's attention. Researchers call this the spotlight effect. Not proof people never notice or judge you. They checked observers' recall against wearers' predictions. What survived outside the wearer's head? Only about 23 percent identified the singer: roughly half the predicted audience. That glance: evidence they noticed, or your own spotlight? Which would you bet on now?
- Sources: Gilovich T., Medvec V.H., Savitsky K., 2000, The Spotlight Effect in Social Judgment: An Egocentric Bias in Estimates of the Salience of One's Own Actions and Appearance, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 78:211-222. Primary evidence for the T-shirt procedure, approximately 46% predicted versus 23% identification, and the proposed anchoring-and-adjustment account. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.78.2.211; Savitsky K., Epley N., Gilovich T., 2001, Do Others Judge Us as Harshly as We Think? Overestimating the Impact of Our Failures, Shortcomings, and Mishaps, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 81:44-56. Supports exaggerated anticipated judgments, discusses the earlier noticing experiments, and distinguishes noticing from evaluation. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.44; Myers D.G., 2014, Myers' Psychology for AP, second edition, Unit 10, page 512, The Spotlight Effect. Independent textbook account of the Barry Manilow procedure and nearly-half prediction versus approximately 23% noticing result. https://phs.phoenix.k12.or.us/uploaded/faculty/Cornet_curriculum/Cornet_PSYCH_curriculum/Myers%27_Psychology_for_AP_-_David_G._Myers.pdf

## Why Does the Stroop Effect Slow You Down? (Try 3 Rounds)
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/stroop_effect/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/qz8KVlP4wpM
- Transcript: You see RED, but your answer should be blue. Before these 3 rounds end, can you stop blaming 1 word? Round one: name this patch's color aloud. Easy? Keep that answer ready; the next round changes something. Round two: name the ink, ignoring the word. Predict whether you'll hesitate. Don't change the rule. If you stumbled, would you blame yourself, or accuse the test of cheating? Choose your culprit. But here's the strange part: reading the word usually suffers much less from conflicting ink. Why the imbalance? Researchers debate the explanation. Reading habits matter, but automatic reading alone isn't a complete account. Round three reverses your job: read the word instead. Same conflict; a different demand. The ink is blue; the word is RED. Competing information disrupts color naming more than word reading. A hesitation needn't mean you failed. You saw the ink; the word challenged your control.
- Sources: Stroop, J. R. (1935). Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 18(6), 643–662. https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Stroop/ — Primary evidence for stronger interference from conflicting words during color naming than from conflicting ink during word reading; practice effects constrain an absolute loss-of-control interpretation.; MacLeod, C. M. (1991). Half a century of research on the Stroop effect: An integrative review. Psychological Bulletin, 109(2), 163–203. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2034749/ — Reviews the interference asymmetry, automaticity, practice and competing explanations; neither simple relative-speed nor automatic-reading explanations fully account for the findings. https://melaniestefan.net/MacLeod1991.pdf; MacLeod, C. M., & MacDonald, P. A. (2000). Interdimensional interference in the Stroop effect: Uncovering the cognitive and neural anatomy of attention. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 4(10), 383–391. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11025281/ — Additional support for interference between relevant and irrelevant dimensions and the role of relative automaticity. The three rounds are demonstrations, not measured individual results; no viewer delay or accuracy is asserted.

## Why Do Unfinished Tasks Interrupt You? (The Planning Twist)
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/zeigarnik_effect/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/qr7ffJa0z-g
- Transcript: Your unfinished 2:00 task could interrupt your 3:00 reading. But how could you stop it before finishing? You probably think finishing is the only escape. Predict: finish, or make a plan? Picture an unfinished email bursting into your book. That envelope behind you matters. But why? Researchers found unfinished goals could intrude during reading. Yet remembering unfinished tasks better is different. But here's the strange part: a recent meta-analysis found no general memory advantage. What survived? A tendency to resume interrupted tasks. Being drawn back isn't proof you remember better. Then what? In planning experiments, participants specified how, when, and where they'd continue. Their tasks stayed unfinished. Then? The reported interference disappeared. If you predicted a plan, you picked the result. But that envelope? It represents a return plan, not completion. Planning helped here; it's no universal guarantee. Your unfinished task remained. Reading could continue. That envelope was an exit without finishing.
- Sources: Zeigarnik, B. (1927). Das Behalten erledigter und unerledigter Handlungen. Psychologische Forschung, 9, 1-85. Historical source for the unfinished-task memory claim; not treated as an established universal effect.; Masicampo, E. J., & Baumeister, R. F. (2010). Unfulfilled goals interfere with tasks that require executive functions. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 46, 994-1006. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2010.06.011 — supports interference from unfulfilled goals.; Masicampo, E. J., & Baumeister, R. F. (2011). Consider it done! Plan making can eliminate the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(4), 667-683. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21688924/ — reading intrusion and specific-plan findings across experiments; the narrated outcome is explicitly limited to these experiments.; Ghibellini, R., & Meier, B. (2025). Interruption, recall and resumption: a meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 12, 962. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-025-05000-w — no general unfinished-task memory advantage; supports a tendency to resume interrupted tasks.; Ovsiankina, M. (1928). Die Wiederaufnahme unterbrochener Handlungen. Psychologische Forschung, 11, 302-379. Historical experimental source for interrupted-task resumption, distinguished from recall.; Masicampo, E. J., & Baumeister, R. F. (2012). Committed but Closed-Minded: When Making a Specific Plan for a Goal Hinders Success. Social Cognition, 30(1), 37-55. https://guilfordjournals.com/doi/10.1521/soco.2012.30.1.37 — supports limits on treating specific plans as universally beneficial.; Production clarification: 2:00 and 3:00 are illustrative everyday times, not experimental measurements. Envelopes, paper intrusions, pathways and arches are visual metaphors, not literal brain structures or measured mechanisms.

## Why Do Onions Make You Cry? (The Missing Enzyme)
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/onion_tears/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/8L7pxdQrKo0
- Transcript: Your onion tears hid 1 enzyme's role until 2002. What did scientists miss before learning how to stop your tears? The sting starts with broken onion cells. Chemicals that were kept apart can finally mix. An enzyme called alliinase breaks down sulfur compounds, producing a reactive ingredient called sulfenic acid. Scientists thought this ingredient became the tear-maker spontaneously. They knew the starting material and the result. The step between them looked like it needed no enzyme. But here's the strange part: that ingredient has another destination. Making tears is only one chemical route. Lachrymatory-factor synthase, identified in 2002, redirects sulfenic acid into the tear-triggering chemical. That was the missing enzyme. That chemical evaporates, reaches your eyes, and irritates them. The result is the familiar flood of tears. In 2008, researchers silenced the enzyme's gene. Experimental onions produced far less of the eye irritant. More precursor went into other sulfur compounds. The chemistry was rerouted, not erased. Your onion tears depended on a chemical detour. Scientists had missed the enzyme at the junction.
- Sources: Imai S. et al., 2002, Plant biochemistry: An onion enzyme that makes the eyes water, Nature 419:685. Supports s1, s4, s6 and s10: discovery of lachrymatory-factor synthase and correction of the spontaneous-formation hypothesis. [Original paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/419685a).; Eady CC et al., 2008, Silencing Onion Lachrymatory Factor Synthase Causes a Significant Change in the Sulfur Secondary Metabolite Profile, Plant Physiology 147:2096–2106. Supports s2–s10: tissue-damage chemistry, enzyme-dependent irritant production, gene silencing, reduced lachrymatory factor and redirected sulfur metabolites. [Full paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2492635/).; Silvaroli JA et al., 2017, Enzyme That Makes You Cry–Crystal Structure of Lachrymatory Factor Synthase from Allium cepa, ACS Chemical Biology 12:2296–2304. Corroborates s1–s10: historical discovery, alliinase and synthase reactions, competing chemical routes, volatile eye irritant and consequences of synthase suppression. [Full paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5693239/).; American Chemical Society / Reactions, 2016, Why Do Onions Make You Cry? Additional support for s2, s3, s6 and s7: onion-cell damage, chemical reactions and tear-triggering irritant. [Official video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RaZpPwmWZ7Q).

## Why Can Roman Concrete Heal Cracks? (Inside the 2023 Test)
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/roman_concrete/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/9k-0ZjXiYv0
- Transcript: You risk discarding Roman concrete's repair material as waste. But why did MIT's 2023 mix stop your 0.5-millimeter leak? The Pantheon's dome is nearly two thousand years old. It remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome. This study examined mortar from Privernum, not the Pantheon. White lumps inside the samples looked like manufacturing mistakes. Researchers had blamed such lumps on poor mixing. The team investigated whether they were evidence of something else. But here's the strange part: a crack could expose its own repair supply. Those white lumps were lime clasts. The study linked them to hot mixing with quicklime. Adding water releases heat, leaving reactive calcium reserves. Later, water entering a crack can dissolve calcium from exposed clasts. Calcium carbonate then crystallizes inside the gap. In Roman-inspired laboratory samples, cracks around half a millimeter wide sealed against water flow. Clast-free controls kept leaking. The test demonstrated sealing; it didn't establish restored structural strength. Nor does it settle every Roman recipe. The experiment reframes the flaw: what looks like waste could be Roman concrete's repair material.
- Sources: Linda M. Seymour et al., 2023, [Hot mixing: Mechanistic insights into the durability of ancient Roman concrete](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9821858/), Science Advances 9(1), eadd1602, doi:10.1126/sciadv.add1602. Supports the Privernum analysis, hot-mixing interpretation, calcium-reservoir mechanism, approximately 0.5-millimeter experimental cracks, calcite precipitation and water-flow measurements in s1 and s3-s10; the demonstrated endpoint is crack sealing rather than recovered structural strength.; David L. Chandler / MIT News, 2023, [Riddle solved: Why was Roman concrete so durable?](https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106). Supports the Pantheon context in s2 and the lime-clast interpretation, hot-mixing chemistry, proposed self-healing mechanism and leaking control comparison in s1 and s3-s10; reports the same research rather than an independent replication.; Sarah Derouin / American Society of Civil Engineers, 2023, [Roman concrete offers lessons in longevity](https://www.asce.org/publications-and-news/civil-engineering-source/civil-engineering-magazine/article/2023/03/roman-concrete-offers-lessons-in-longevity/). Researcher interview and technical account supporting the reactive-calcium mechanism, hot mixing and experimentally healed cracks up to 0.5 millimeters in s1 and s4-s8.; Guinness World Records, publication year unspecified, accessed 2026, [Largest masonry dome](https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/83547-largest-masonry-dome). Supports the Pantheon's second-century construction and record dome span in s2, alongside MIT News; no exact completion year is asserted.

## Why Can't You Tickle Yourself? (The Robot Delay Test)
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/tickle_yourself/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/M7aGhp0eWXI
- Transcript: Your robotic self-tickle can fail with 0 milliseconds of added delay. But before you quit, what changes at 200? Mira meets a robot tickler. She expects a machine to beat her own defenses. In the experiment, movement of the left hand controlled a robot stimulating the right palm. With no added delay, people rated that touch less tickly than externally produced touch. But here's the strange part: with 200 milliseconds added, participants rated the same touch ticklier. The robot didn't tickle harder. Only the timing relative to the movement changed. The proposed explanation: your brain predicts sensations from your movement and dampens matching touch. A delayed touch mismatches that forecast. Less dampening lets more tickliness through. Researchers measured tickliness ratings, not a guaranteed burst of laughter. Timing changed perception. Mira's robotic self-tickle didn't need more force. It needed to miss her brain's appointment.
- Sources: Blakemore S-J, Wolpert DM, Frith CD, 1998, Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation, Nature Neuroscience 1(7):635–640. [Original research](https://doi.org/10.1038/2870). Supports reduced responses to self-produced touch and the prediction-based explanation.; Blakemore S-J, Frith CD, Wolpert DM, 1999, Spatio-Temporal Prediction Modulates the Perception of Self-Produced Stimuli, Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience 11(5):551–559. [Original research](https://doi.org/10.1162/089892999563607). Supports the paired-robot setup, zero added delay comparison, increased tickliness ratings at 200 milliseconds, unchanged tactile stimulation across delay conditions, and ratings rather than guaranteed laughter.; Blakemore S-J, Wolpert DM, Frith CD, 2000, Why can't you tickle yourself?, NeuroReport 11(11):R11–R16. [Research review](https://doi.org/10.1097/00001756-200008030-00002). Corroborates the paired-robot setup, increased tickliness ratings between zero and 200 milliseconds, unchanged tactile stimulation, and predictive sensory attenuation. Mira's visit is a fictional dramatization; the brain's appointment is a metaphor.

## Why Does Cornstarch Feel Solid When You Hit It?
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/cornstarch_impact_jamming/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/piZzfiZDeb8
- Transcript: Your fingers stir this kitchen goo easily, but your foot may meet resistance. Why? Everyone says stuff is solid or liquid. This goo ignores the rule. Press slowly, and your foot sinks like soup. Hit it fast, and it feels like a floor. Inside, starch grains drift in water, sliding past each other like a calm crowd. But here's the strange part: your hit builds the wall. Grains get shoved together, and a jammed patch races outward in thousandths of a second. Picture a panicked crowd at one doorway. Nobody can move, so the mass pushes back. Scientists still debate how much comes from jammed grain chains and how much from other stresses. Stop moving and the wall melts back to liquid. Nothing is trapping you. Next time your fingers stir kitchen goo, hit it fast. You will notice it tonight.
- Sources: Waitukaitis & Jaeger, 2012, Impact-activated solidification of dense suspensions via dynamic jamming fronts, Nature 487:205-209 (mechanism of jamming front; contribution of other stresses is still debated); Brown & Jaeger, 2014, Shear thickening in concentrated suspensions: phenomenology, mechanisms and relations to jamming, Reports on Progress in Physics 77:046602 (several mechanisms compete; no single settled answer); Sources were model-suggested: verify before publishing, including the 'thousandths of a second' timescale.

## Why Doesn't Freezing Kill This Frog?
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/wood_frog_freeze_survival/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/BQQUHnJengE
- Transcript: You see ice outside a frog's cells. So why doesn't the freeze kill it? As ice grows between cells, water shifts outward. Pressure can damage shrinking cells. The liver senses ice and breaks stored glycogen into glucose, then releases that sugar into the blood. Glucose helps protect tissues as water shifts, cushioning cells and limiting some damage. But here's the strange part: the heart can stop and breathing pause while much of the frog freezes. Yet most cells do not become solid ice. Ice forms mainly outside them, and glucose helps reduce harm from the squeeze. When warmth returns, ice melts. The heart may beat again, and the frog may move. How organs manage repeated freeze-thaw cycles remains under study. Ice surrounds the cells, then melts; the frog can return to motion.
- Sources: Janet M. Storey and Kenneth B. Storey, 1985, Triggering of cryoprotectant synthesis by the initiation of ice nucleation in the freeze tolerant frog Rana sylvatica, Journal of Comparative Physiology B 156:191–195.; Kenneth B. Storey and Janet B. Storey, 1986, Freeze tolerance and intolerance as strategies of winter survival in terrestrially-hibernating amphibians, Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology A 83(4):613–617.; Kenneth B. Storey, 1987, Organ-specific metabolism during freezing and thawing in a freeze-tolerant frog, American Journal of Physiology 253:R292–R297.

## Sand Looks Solid. So How Does This Lizard Swim?
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/sandfish_swims_through_sand/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/LcNc83G6c2I
- Transcript: Your fingers make ripples in a bowl. But one wave travels through a buried lizard. Why doesn't sand stop it? Look at your thumb. Press it into your palm. Feel that firm push? Sand pushes back too, so legs would just plow. But the sandfish pins its legs to its sides. Remember one number: one fifth. X-rays caught it. A bend runs head to tail, therefore each curve shoves grains back, and grains shove the body forward. But here's the strange part: that fifth is how tall each bend stands beside its length. Any deeper wastes effort, models suggest. Scientists still debate details, because the best model depends on how tightly the grains are packed. So sand isn't a wall. Pushed just right, it flows like a thick fluid. Your ripple, buried. Same wave. Different ocean. Your bowl ripples; the desert ripples back.
- Sources: Ryan D. Maladen et al., 2009, Undulatory Swimming in Sand: Subsurface Locomotion of the Sandfish Lizard, Science 325:314-318 (X-ray imaging of real animals; model-suggested citation, verify before publishing); Ryan D. Maladen et al., 2011, Mechanical Models of Sandfish Locomotion Reveal Principles of High Performance Subsurface Sand-Swimming, Journal of the Royal Society Interface 8:1332-1345 (robot and simulation models; the best force model depends on grain packing, and the one-fifth bend ratio is a model result, verify before publishing)

## How Can 4 Stickers Make AI Read STOP as 45?
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/sticker_turns_stop_sign/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/W_VmzUbnNv4
- Transcript: Your eyes read STOP. But how could stickers make one classifier see Speed Limit 45? Everyone assumes the car sees a sign. It doesn't. It sees a grid of numbers. Layer by layer, those numbers become one score per sign. Stop usually wins. But four small stickers nudge those scores. Stop slips. Speed Limit climbs. Therefore the car crosses an invisible line, a decision boundary, and the answer flips. But here's the strange part: experts still argue why this works. Some say the model is fragile, like a bridge with one weak bolt. Others say it spots real patterns we can't. Both have evidence. Therefore the machine isn't dumb. It's just reading differently. The relief: engineers can train cars against these tricks, making them harder to fool. Next time you see STOP, remember: your eyes read it. A car must decide.
- Sources: Eykholt K, Evtimov I, Fernandes E, Li B, Rahmati A, Xiao C, Prakash A, Kohno T, Song D, 2018, Robust Physical-World Attacks on Deep Learning Visual Classification, CVPR 2018:1625-1634 (stickers on real signs fooled classifiers; results depend on the model and test setup); Szegedy C, Zaremba W, Sutskever I, Bruna J, Erhan D, Goodfellow I, Fergus R, 2014, Intriguing properties of neural networks, ICLR 2014 (arXiv:1312.6199) (first showed tiny input changes can flip a network's answer); Ilyas A, Santurkar S, Tsipras D, Engstrom L, Tran B, Madry A, 2019, Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features, NeurIPS 32 (argues they exploit real but human-invisible patterns; this view is still debated)

## Why Does Rain Smell Like Dirt? (It's Not Just Soil)
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/rain_launches_soil_aerosols/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/BKd4J4IKx8o
- Transcript: Your nose calls it wet dirt after rain. But what does a raindrop do before the smell reaches you? A raindrop doesn't just stir a smell already in dry soil. It spreads water across pores and traps air underneath. That air gathers into bubbles. Pressure drives them upward through narrow spaces between grains, toward the water's surface. At the top, a bubble bursts. The pop can eject droplets carrying soil material into the air. A splash becomes a launch. But here's the strange part: airborne particles can carry ground material, yet they don't explain every note in rain's scent. The smell varies with soil, weather, and odor-producing compounds. Bubbles offer one route for material to travel, not the whole recipe. Think of a bubble as a soil catapult, sending ground material airborne. Next rain, watch for the pop before your nose names the smell.
- Sources: Joung, Y. S. & Buie, C. R., 2015, “Aerosol generation by raindrop impact on soil,” Nature Communications 6:6083. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms7083 — demonstrates aerosol generation on porous surfaces; its contribution to the smell people notice can vary.; Bear, I. J. & Thomas, R. G., 1964, “Nature of Argillaceous Odour,” Nature 201:993–995. https://doi.org/10.1038/201993a0 — describes the variable nature of petrichor.

## Why Does Spaghetti Keep Snapping After the First Crack?
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/spaghetti_fracture_cascade/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/qMRwV9z2kiA
- Transcript: Your dry spaghetti breaks in your hands. But why doesn't the first crack finish the job? Bending stores elastic energy. A crack launches a fast bending wave toward both ends. The wave briefly bends each fragment again. That extra bend can focus stress at a weak spot before the first piece settles. But here's the strange part: the first crack starts a cascade. Each wave reshapes the strand, so the next break depends on its bend at that instant. A snap sends a shiver down the rod. Where motion meets a flaw, the local bend can spike and trigger another fracture. Twisting changes the race. A twist wave can travel faster than a bending wave, reducing extra bending that drives repeated cracks. Results depend on setup. Flaws and bending conditions still matter, so results vary. Next time spaghetti cracks, watch the remaining strand: it may not be finished.
- Sources: Basile Audoly and Sébastien Neukirch, 2005, “Fragmentation of Rods by Cascading Cracks: Why Spaghetti Does Not Break in Half,” Physical Review Letters 95, 095505. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.095505; Ronald H. Heisser, Vishal P. Patil, Norbert Stoop, Emmanuel Villermaux, and Jörn Dunkel, 2018, “Controlling fracture cascades through twisting and quenching,” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115, 8665–8670. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1802831115

## Why Your Phone's GPS Needs a Slow Clock
- Companion Page: https://yigitkoc2005-cloud.github.io/parallax-science/shorts/gps_clocks_need_relativity/
- YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/mcRSZH8IBI8
- Transcript: Your phone's map is quietly rescued from a clock problem you can't see. Can you guess how? GPS finds you by timing satellite signals. A clock error becomes a distance error. Two effects pull opposite ways. Weaker gravity makes satellite clocks tick faster. Their speed slows them down. But here's the strange part: gravity wins. Together, satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds each day—enough to create roughly eleven kilometers of range error. The fix starts before launch: satellite clocks are preset to tick slow. Your receiver corrects smaller shifts as the orbit changes. Think of runners sending timed flashes. A racing watch makes each flash seem farther away. Your phone compares satellite signal times to find your position. So who gets blamed: your map or the clock in the sky? Would you trust Einstein with your directions, or call it a clock problem?
- Sources: Ashby, Neil, 2003, “Relativity in the Global Positioning System,” Living Reviews in Relativity 6, article 1.; Ashby, Neil & Marc Weiss, 2013, “Why There Is No Noon-Midnight Red Shift in the GPS,” arXiv:1307.6525.
